questions.q: What does a maintainability NFR primarily measure?
options: How easily the system can be understood, modified, and extended safely, ideally by someone other than its original builder
How fast the system responds to user actions
How many records the system can hold before performance degrades
Whether the system meets a specific regulatory certification
questions.explain: Maintainability is about whether a system can be safely changed and extended by someone other than the original builder, without unexpected breakage — not about speed, capacity, or regulatory status.

questions.q: Why can an org with poor maintainability look completely fine from the outside?
options: Because maintainability issues always cause immediate visible outages
Because Salesforce automatically flags maintainability problems in Setup

Because it can still do what it's supposed to do today — the cost of poor maintainability shows up later, when someone has to safely change it and discovers undocumented, duplicated, or poorly understood logic
Because maintainability only matters for orgs with over 1 million records
questions.explain: An org can function correctly in its current state while still being very difficult to safely change — the maintainability cost is deferred until the next person has to modify it and discovers undocumented or tangled logic.

questions.q: Why are maintainability and recoverability grouped together in this course despite describing different things?
options: Because they are actually the same NFR measured two different ways
Because both are about the organization's ability to safely act on the system after go-live, rather than about end-user-facing behavior in the moment
Because Salesforce Shield licenses both features as a single bundle
Because they are both measured using the same governor limits
questions.explain: Maintainability is about safely changing the system after go-live; recoverability is about safely returning to a known-good state after something goes wrong post go-live. Both point at the same root cause: insufficient investment in what happens after the initial build, distinct from in-the-moment end-user experience.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's native Backup and Restore product provide, per this lesson?
options: Real-time field-level encryption for sensitive data
A CPU-time governor limit override for high-volume batch jobs
A role-hierarchy recalculation tool for large user bases
Automated backups of standard and custom object data, encrypted at rest and in transit, with the ability to restore backed-up data into an org and log auditing of backup and restore actions
questions.explain: Backup and Restore is Salesforce's native backup product, supporting automated, encrypted backups of standard and custom object data, restore of backed-up data into an org, and audit logging of backup and restore activity.

questions.q: A client makes all configuration changes directly in production, with no sandbox or version control. Which maintainability tool from this lesson most directly addresses the risk this creates?
options: Source control and a deployment pipeline using sandboxes or scratch orgs, so changes are validated and reviewed before reaching production
Salesforce Backup and Restore
Field Audit Trail
Big Objects
questions.explain: Making changes directly in production with no version control or testing environment is exactly the risk a source-control and sandbox-based deployment pipeline is designed to close — turning changes into a reviewable, versioned, testable process instead of untracked edits to live data.
